Based on the specific astronomical data you provided, the short answer is: **It is highly unlikely that you would be able to see the Moon with your unaided eyes.**

Here is the breakdown of why you can probably relax:

### 1. The "Washout" Effect (Solar Glare)
The most significant factor is the Sun's position. With an altitude of **68.3 degrees**, the Sun is very high in the sky. Even though the Moon is in a different part of the sky (Azimuth 114° vs. Sun's 243°), the sheer amount of scattered sunlight in a "clear" sky creates a high level of ambient brightness. In "bright daylight," the contrast required to see a celestial body is usually lost.

### 2. Low Altitude and Atmospheric Extinction
The Moon is at an altitude of only **12.2 degrees**. This means it is relatively low toward the horizon. When a celestial object is that low, its light must pass through a much thicker layer of the Earth's atmosphere. This causes "atmospheric extinction," which dims the object significantly.

### 3. Phase and Illumination
At **50.95% illumination**, the Moon is in a "Quarter" phase. While this is a distinct shape, it is not a Full Moon. Because it is only half-lit, it lacks the maximum surface area of reflected light needed to punch through the daytime glare of a clear sky.

### 4. The Geometry
The Moon is about 90 degrees away from the Sun. While this means it isn't "hidden" behind the Sun's glare (like it would be during a New Moon), it also means it is sitting in the bright, blue part of the daytime sky. Unless there is a very specific atmospheric condition (like heavy haze or smoke) that dulls the blue of the sky while letting the Moon's light through, the Moon will simply blend into the blue.

### Verdict:
Because you are an "ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight," you would need the Moon to be much higher in the sky or much closer to a Full Moon phase to spot it during the day. At 12 degrees high in broad daylight, **it will almost certainly be invisible to you.** 

You can breathe a sigh of relief!
